title: Is ragtime dying, and its leading exponents
summary: He thinks ragtime will survive and names Wally Rose and Max Morath.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: If I can focus for just a minute on a couple of questions pertinent to ragtime, do you think that ragtime is a dying art? Do you think that it's something that's bound to die out as the present experts become fewer and fewer in number like yourself? Do you think that it's a genre that's going to be submerged ultimately and disappear?

No, Charlie, I don't think it will disappear because there are too many people interested in it today. And there are too many jazz clubs throughout the country. For instance, California, you have clubs out there who are devoted entirely to this form of music. And I really don't think that it will ever completely die out because it's sort of something, a tradition, that people just don't want to let die.
Would this be too difficult to ask you in just a second, who do you consider to be, say, three of the greatest exponents of ragtime alive today?

Three of the greatest ragtime exponents alive today? Well, that's really a question, Charlie. I know there is a fellow by the name of Wally Rose who is considered a real great ragtime pianist. And then you have this Max Morath who has been on educational TV who really plays a real bang-up ragtime piano. And, well, I can't think just offhand, but there are several pianists around who are really playing real fine ragtime. I mean, they can, they really do a real good job. Okay.
